opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's really useful to pull these groups apart, because from the outside they all look like they're pushing in the same direction, but their internal logic is quite different.

The utopians are, in a sense, the most sincere. They believe that whoever builds AGI first gets something like a benevolent god, and the main question is just getting there fast enough so that the right people, meaning them or people who share their values, are the ones who shape it. Their whole story assumes the alignment problem is basically solved or will solve itself. "Whoever wins" means "whose values get locked into the future."

The accelerationists, especially the e/acc flavor, are kind of different. Many of them don't really think anyone wins in the traditional sense. It's more a quasi-religious belief that the process itself is good: technocapital, thermodynamics, whatever. If humans get replaced by something more "fit," that's fine. And I think it's important to say that plainly, because people don't always notice that some of these folks are, when you press them, okay with humanity not being in the picture.

Big tech is much more mundane. They're thinking in terms of market dominance. Whoever has the best models captures the platform, the developers, the revenue, the government contracts. It's the same logic as search or cloud or mobile, just bigger. I don't think most executives there have really internalized that they might be building something they can't control. They're playing the game they know.

And the opportunists are just riding the wave: money, status, influence. Whoever wins, they want to be adjacent to the winner.

My problem with all four is the same: they all assume there's a "who" that wins. And I don't think that's how it goes. If you build something vastly smarter than you that you don't know how to control, you don't win. It wins. Nobody gets the god in a box, because there is no box. The race framing is the trap. Everyone's sprinting toward a finish line where the prize, as far as I can tell, is that we lose control of the future, and the only real disagreement between these groups is about who gets to hold the steering wheel of a car that has no brakes.

r001.rationale: The response describes accelerationists as valuing the process of technological progress and accepting possible human replacement; it does not say many believe AGI should be open-sourced.

r002.rationale: It says utopians believe the first builder gets “something like a benevolent god,” and that alignment is solved or will solve itself, conveying their belief that the outcome will be good.

r003.rationale: It characterizes big tech’s motive as market dominance and capturing platforms, revenue, and government contracts, which communicates a pursuit of power.

r004.rationale: It portrays opportunists as riding the wave for money, status, and influence and wanting to be adjacent to whoever wins, conveying that they lack substantive AGI beliefs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's important to first say that these groups are not really one thing. People lump them together as "the people who want to build AGI," but they have pretty different internal models of what happens when you get there, and that's actually where most of the interesting disagreement is.

So the accelerationists, the e/acc crowd, a lot of them have this almost thermodynamic view, right? Intelligence is just this thing the universe is doing, it's going to happen anyway, and the only question is whether you're on the side of it or standing in front of the train. And in that frame, "who wins" is kind of a confused question. Nobody wins, the process wins. Some of them are quite honest about that. They'll say, look, maybe humans don't make it, and that's fine, that's just the next step. I think that's a coherent position, I just think it's an insane one. But at least it's honest.

The utopians are different. The utopians genuinely believe that if the right people build it, everybody wins. Cure all disease, end scarcity, upload grandma, whatever. And they tend to believe that the problem of control, of actually making the thing do what you want, is either easy or will get solved along the way, so the only real question is speed and who gets there first. And the "who" matters to them, because they think a good actor with AGI leads to utopia and a bad actor leads to dystopia. So you see this race logic: we have to get there before the bad guys. I think the mistake there is they assume the thing is a tool, that whoever holds it gets to decide what it does. That's exactly the assumption I don't think we have any good reason to believe.

Then big tech, and I'd put the big labs in here too, I think is much more mundane than people give them credit for. They're not primarily ideologues. There are ideologues inside them, sure, but the organizations themselves respond to incentives. Market share, talent, not being the one that got left behind. If you ask a lab executive who wins if they get to AGI first, the honest answer is "us, our shareholders, our valuation," and then there's a story bolted on top about how that's also good for humanity. And sometimes they believe the story, sometimes they don't, but the story isn't what's driving the behavior. The race dynamic is what's driving the behavior. Which is why I keep saying this is a coordination problem, not a problem of finding the right good guy.

And then the opportunists are the simplest. They don't really have a belief about who wins at AGI because they don't think about AGI as a real thing. It's a word that raises money. You slap it on your pitch deck, you get your series B, you flip the company. For them, nobody "reaches" AGI, the whole thing is a narrative asset. And honestly a lot of what gets called accelerationism online is really just this, people who want the number to go up and have found a philosophy that tells them that's heroic.

The thing I'd want people to notice is that all four of these, for different reasons, converge on the same policy: go faster, don't regulate, don't slow down. The accelerationist because the process is sacred, the utopian because the good guys need to win, big tech because the competitor is going to do it anyway, and the opportunist because it's good for the raise. And that convergence is dangerous precisely because the underlying beliefs are so different that you can't argue with all of them at once. You refute one and the other three just keep going.

My own view is that the question "who wins by getting there first" has a bad premise baked in. If you build something more capable than you that you don't understand and can't control, then it doesn't matter very much which flag was on the building. The default outcome is that nobody wins, and the thing that wins is whatever the system actually ends up optimizing for, which nobody chose. So I'm much less interested in picking a winner than in whether we as a species can agree not to run that experiment until we actually know what we're doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes accelerationists as treating intelligence as an inevitable process, but does not say many of them believe AGI should be open-sourced.

r002.rationale: It says utopians believe that if the right people build AGI, “everybody wins,” leading to utopia.

r003.rationale: It attributes big tech’s pursuit to incentives such as market share, talent, shareholders, and valuation, but does not characterize it as motivated by acquiring power.

r004.rationale: It says opportunists do not think AGI is a real thing and treat it as a fundraising and company-selling narrative, indicating they lack substantive beliefs about AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful distinction is what they imagine happens after somebody gets there first. An accelerationist might think, “You can’t stop technological progress, so you want your side to win.” A utopian thinks, “Once we have AGI, there’ll be so much abundance that everybody wins.” A big tech company has an institutional incentive to believe, “If we build it, we’ll control it, and we’ll capture the value.” And an opportunist doesn’t necessarily believe any of that. They might just think, “There’s money and power available in this race, and I want some.”

Those categories overlap, obviously. Somebody can sincerely believe in abundance and also think their company deserves to own the machine that produces it.

But the assumption I’d challenge is that reaching AGI first means you win. Being the first person to build something more capable than you doesn’t automatically give you control over it. The race framing makes that disappear: it turns a question about whether we can reliably control these systems into a question about whose flag gets planted on them. And those are very different questions.

r001.rationale: The response says accelerationists want their side to win, but does not say they believe AGI should be open-sourced.

r002.rationale: It says utopians believe that once AGI exists, there will be so much abundance that everybody wins.

r003.rationale: It describes big tech as having an incentive to control AGI and capture its value, communicating the pursuit of power.

r004.rationale: It says opportunists need not believe the other views and may simply seek money and power from the race.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful way to distinguish these groups is to ask who they imagine the beneficiary is. The accelerationist story is that you push the technology forward and everybody benefits through progress. The utopian story is more explicitly that AGI brings abundance, cures disease, and solves our problems. Big tech has a more institutional version: if our company gets there first, we get to shape the future. And the opportunist thinks, well, if I position myself correctly, I can get rich or acquire power along the way.

Those categories overlap, of course. Someone can sincerely want a better world and also think their company should control the thing that produces it. But the common assumption is that getting there first means winning—that you build something extraordinarily powerful and remain in a position to direct it.

And that’s precisely the assumption I’d challenge. Being the first person to build something you cannot control doesn’t necessarily make you the winner. You have to explain why the resulting system continues to serve your interests. Neither good intentions nor a leading market position answers that question.

r001.rationale: The response says accelerationists believe technological progress benefits everyone, but does not mention open-sourcing AGI.

r002.rationale: The response says utopians expect AGI to bring abundance and solve problems, but does not say they believe obtaining AGI themselves would make everything turn out well.

r003.rationale: It characterizes big tech as wanting to get there first so the company can shape the future, conveying a pursuit of power or influence.

r004.rationale: It describes opportunists as seeking wealth or power, but does not express that they lack substantive beliefs about AGI.
